strengths: QuEST addresses an important deployment problem with a practical strategy: finetune sensitive time-embedding and attention-related layers using full-precision model supervision. Updating approximately 7% of LDM-4 parameters without requiring the original training images is potentially useful.

The low-bit results show meaningful empirical gains. In Table 3, W4A4 FID improves over EfficientDM from 10.60 to 5.64 on LSUN-Bedrooms and from 14.34 to 11.76 on LSUN-Churches. These improvements are valuable even without uniformly leading every benchmark.

Evaluation spans unconditional, class-conditional, and text-to-image generation across four model configurations. Most quantitative results use 50,000 samples. The activation-distribution visualizations, sensitivity experiments, and component ablations provide useful motivation and supporting evidence.
The manuscript cites its principal datasets and baseline methods, provides a code link and several training settings, and acknowledges relevant implications for watermarking and safety checking.
weaknesses: The claimed theoretical justification is unsound as written. Section 2.3.1 perturbs the final output entering an MSE loss, which is quadratic; its second-order Taylor expansion is therefore exact regardless of perturbation magnitude. Large perturbations do not invalidate that expansion. Furthermore, Appendix B does not justify replacing the perturbation vectors in Equation 10's Hessian term with output residuals in Equation 5. The argument establishes neither finetuning sufficiency nor sufficiency of the selected layers. This undermines the theoretical contribution, although it does not refute the empirical method.

The ImageNet results leave the quality conclusions unresolved. At W4A4, QuEST achieves slightly better FID than EfficientDM, but worse sFID (7.93 versus 7.75) and substantially lower IS (202.45 versus 250.90; full precision is 364.73). The manuscript itself questions FID in this setting, yet does not investigate the disagreement sufficiently. Additional fidelity/diversity analysis is needed to support its interpretation of the results.

The headline Stable Diffusion result has limited validation. Table 5 reports only CLIPScore, falling from 31.50 to 28.85 at W4A4, while Figure 11 covers two prompts. This supports feasibility and some semantic preservation, but does not adequately characterize visual fidelity or diversity. Comparison only against Q-Diffusion also leaves the advantage over competing finetuning approaches unclear.

The distinctive selective and progressive training choices are insufficiently isolated. Teacher supervision, efficient finetuning, and timestep grouping overlap with ideas in the cited literature. Table 7 shows that adding components helps, but lacks a parameter-budget-matched alternative layer selection or a joint-versus-progressive training comparison. Its restriction to W4A8 LSUN-Bedrooms further limits the explanation of the headline W4A4 gains.

The efficiency evidence is narrower than the conclusions. Table 7 demonstrates lower calibration time than Q-Diffusion (15.25 versus 23.08 GPU hours), but higher memory consumption (12,450 versus 10,334 MB), and provides no corresponding EfficientDM cost comparison or measured low-bit inference speed. The phrase 'full 4-bit Stable Diffusion' also needs qualification: attention matrix multiplications and boundary layers remain 8-bit, and quantization targets the U-Net rather than the complete pipeline.

Despite the code link, important reproduction details are missing from the manuscript: quantizer granularity and initialization, gradient treatment through rounding, exact selected layers for each architecture, classifier-free guidance scales, and conditioning used to construct calibration samples. These choices materially affect low-bit performance and the interpretation of the data-free claim.
